title: The Holy Sonnets and this sonnet's place
short: One of Donne's Holy Sonnets, printed in 1633; it is probably of about 1609 and imagines the Last Judgement.
body: The Holy Sonnets were first printed in 1633 and 1635 and survive in different orders in the manuscripts; Grierson, following the editions of 1635 to 1669, numbers this one VII, while in the 1633 set of twelve it comes fourth. Helen Gardner argued that most were written around 1609 to 1610, before Donne's ordination, and grouped this sonnet with others on the Last Things. Louis Martz showed how the sonnets follow the stages of Ignatian meditation: a vivid 'composition of place' (here the Judgement), followed by analysis and a closing prayer. This one opens with a cosmic scene and closes on private repentance.

title: the round earths imagin'd corners
short: From Revelation 7:1, the angels at 'the four corners of the earth'; calling them 'imagin'd' acknowledges that a round earth has no corners.
body: Revelation 7:1 describes four angels standing at 'the four corners of the earth'. Donne, aware that the earth is a globe, calls the corners 'imagin'd': the visionary geography of Scripture is held together with modern cosmology in one paradox. Grierson, quoting the line in his introduction among Donne's 'magnificent openings', prints 'quarters' there, though the text of his edition reads 'corners', as here.

title: blow / Your trumpets, Angells
short: The last trumpet that will wake the dead at the Second Coming.
body: Paul writes that 'the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible' (1 Corinthians 15:52), and that the Lord will descend 'with the trump of God' (1 Thessalonians 4:16); in Matthew 24:31 the angels are sent 'with a great sound of a trumpet' to gather the elect from the four winds. Donne commands the angels as if he were directing the Judgement himself, an audacity the sestet will retract. The doubled imperative 'arise, arise' enacts the summons.

title: you numberlesse infinities / Of soules
short: The countless souls of the dead, too many to number, are called back to their bodies.
body: The phrase multiplies infinity, a characteristic Donne hyperbole. The line break after 'infinities' leaves the word hanging before it is defined as 'soules'. Compare Revelation 7:9, which follows the four angels of 7:1 with 'a great multitude, which no man could number'. The resurrection is pictured as a vast gathering of every soul since Adam, which makes the later turn to one sinner all the more striking.

title: to your scattred bodies goe
short: At the resurrection each soul returns to its own body, whose matter has been scattered by death and decay.
body: Christian doctrine taught the resurrection of the body, not merely the survival of the soul: the soul, separated at death, would be reunited with its own flesh. Theologians debated how God would reassemble bodies whose dust had been scattered, eaten or burned, a question Donne returns to in his sermons. The imperative 'goe' sends the souls down, reversing the usual image of ascent.

anchor: the flood did, and fire shall
title: the flood did, and fire shall o'erthrow
short: Noah's Flood destroyed the first world; fire will destroy the present one at the end of time.
body: The line spans the whole of history in two catastrophes. The Flood is Genesis 6 to 8; the final burning comes from 2 Peter 3:6-7, where the world that 'perished' by water is 'reserved unto fire against the day of judgment', and 2 Peter 3:10, where 'the elements shall melt with fervent heat'. The tenses, past and future ('did ... shall'), place the speaker between them.

title: The catalogue of deaths
short: A rapid list of the ways people die, from war and fevers to despair, the law and mere chance.
body: The lines pile up nouns in a breathless list: 'warre, death, age, agues, tyrannies, / Despaire, law, chance'. 'Agues' are fevers; 'tyrannies' are deaths at the hands of tyrants; 'Despaire' is suicide; 'law' is judicial execution. The enumeration, crossing the line-ending, gives the octave its sweep before the sestet narrows to one sinner. Grammatically the singular 'hath slaine' follows a long plural subject, an irregularity of the period.

title: death / dearth
short: The printed texts read 'death', but the Westmoreland manuscript reads 'dearth' (famine); Grierson and later editors adopted 'dearth'.
body: Grierson argued that 'dearth' must be right: the poet is listing the modes in which death comes, and death itself cannot be one of them. He thought the 'death' of l. 8 ('deaths woe') helped cause the error. Most modern editions, including Gardner's, read 'dearth', meaning famine, which completes a traditional set of scourges with war. This text keeps the 1633 reading 'death'.

title: you whose eyes, / Shall behold God, and never tast deaths woe
short: Those still alive at the Second Coming, who will be changed without dying.
body: Paul says 'We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed' (1 Corinthians 15:51), and those who are 'alive and remain' will be caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The phrase 'taste of death' is from the Gospels (Luke 9:27, Matthew 16:28), where Jesus says some standing there 'shall not taste of death' till they see the kingdom of God. The octave thus embraces the dead of all ages and the living at the end.

title: The volta
short: The sestet reverses the octave: he asks God to delay the Judgement so he has time to repent.
body: The sonnet is Petrarchan in its octave (abbaabba) but closes, as Donne's Holy Sonnets usually do, with a couplet (cdcdee). The turn at l. 9 is sudden: having summoned the trumpets, the speaker now asks that the dead 'sleepe' a while longer, the usual Christian euphemism for death. The cosmic scene shrinks to one man's need: 'and mee mourne a space'. In Martz's terms the move can be read as the shift from composition of place to self-examination in meditation.

title: mourne a space
short: To grieve over his sins for a while: 'a space' means a period of time.
body: 'Space' in the sense of an interval of time was common in the period. Mourning here is penitential sorrow for sin, the first stage of repentance in the theology of the time. The petition for time is ironic, since it asks God to postpone the event the octave had so grandly commanded.

title: my sinnes abound ... abundance of thy grace
short: An echo of Romans 5:20: 'where sin abounded, grace did much more abound'.
body: Donne plays on 'abound' and 'abundance': if his sins exceed all the deaths just listed, he will need more grace than it is safe to ask for at the last moment. Paul's assurance in Romans 5:20 that grace abounds more than sin lies behind the pun, giving a hopeful undertone to the fear. 'Tis late to aske ... When wee are there': once at the Judgement, the time for repentance is past.

title: here on this lowly ground
short: Earth, the place of humility, is where repentance must be learned, as opposed to 'there' at the Judgement.
body: The antithesis of 'there' and 'here' splits the line at its centre. 'Lowly' carries both physical and moral senses: the low earth and the humility proper to penitence. The opening's vast globe has contracted to the ground the speaker stands on. The phrase also recalls that Adam was formed 'of the dust of the ground' (Genesis 2:7), so that 'lowly ground' is both the place and the material of fallen humanity, where alone repentance can be learned before the trumpets sound.

title: Teach mee how to repent
short: He asks God for the very ability to repent, since in Protestant theology even repentance is a gift of grace.
body: In the Reformed theology of Donne's Church, a sinner cannot repent by his own power; contrition is itself God's work. The plea therefore asks for grace at its root. The final couplet claims that true repentance is 'as good' as a sealed pardon: being taught to repent is the evidence that one is already forgiven. Critics differ on how far the Holy Sonnets reflect Calvinist anxiety about election; the couplet here is comparatively confident.

title: seal'd my pardon, with thy blood
short: Christ's blood is imagined as the seal on a legal pardon, making it valid.
body: A royal pardon was valid only when sealed. Donne makes Christ's blood the sealing wax, drawing on the Epistle to the Hebrews, where Christ's blood ratifies the new covenant (Hebrews 9:12-22: 'without shedding of blood is no remission'). The sonnet ends with a legal image of assurance after the terror of the Judgement. The paradox is that the blood which seals the pardon has already been shed; what the speaker needs is to be taught to repent, which is 'as good' as the seal.
